blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The null hypothesis (H₀) is the claim assumed true for the test. It fixes a value of the parameter, so that the sampling distribution of the statistic can be worked out. Usually that value is “no effect”: a difference of 0 or a ratio of 1. The alternative hypothesis (H₁ or Hₐ) covers the other possible values: the effect, difference or association the researcher is usually looking for.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: H₀ has to name a value because the test needs a sampling distribution to compare the data with, and a sampling distribution needs a centre (recall §6.5). “The difference is 0” gives one; “there is some difference” does not. That is why the sceptical, precise claim is the one tested, and H₁ is supported only indirectly, by evidence against H₀.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
For the urban–rural weights of §7.2.3: H₀: μ_urban − μ_rural = 0; H₁: μ_urban − μ_rural ≠ 0.

H₀ need not say “no effect”. To ask whether a district’s mean birthweight differs from a reference value of 3.0 kg, the hypotheses are H₀: μ = 3.0 kg and H₁: μ ≠ 3.0 kg (the one-sample tests of §9.1 and §9.2.1). In a non-inferiority trial (a trial designed to show that a new treatment is not worse than the standard by more than a stated margin M, §15.9), the null is “the new treatment is worse by M or more”, and H₁ is “it is worse by less than M, or better” (ICH, 1998). Greenland et al. (2016) call the general case the test hypothesis; the “no effect” null is its most common form.

points.html: H₀ is usually “no difference / no association”, but it can be any stated value: a reference mean, a target coverage, a non-inferiority margin.
The test only ever assesses evidence against H₀. It never proves H₁, and failing to reject H₀ does not prove H₀ (recall §8.1).
H₀ and H₁ are mutually exclusive and together cover every possible value of the parameter, so rejecting one supports the other.
Whether H₁ specifies a direction (“the drug improves recovery”) or not (“the drug changes recovery”) decides whether the test is one-tailed or two-tailed (§8.6).
